title: Daisy Dolittle

subtitle.text: "Attention, please!" an old elephant called.
"Let's start this meeting of the Council of Animals."
The elephant stood on a rocky beach between an ocean and a forest.
A magpie, a sea turtle, and a pig were gathered before her.
Any person who saw them would wonder how they had come to be there together.
But no human had ever set foot on this beach.
It was a place of strong magic known only to animals.
A bumblebee was also there, though she wasn't sure why.
"Thank you for coming, my striped friend," the turtle said.
The bee buzzed nervously.
"Are you sure you meant to summon me
?" "Yes," the elephant
said. "Our current problem affects all animals
worldwide. You see, humans are forgetting that the earth belongs to all of
us." The magpie hopped
forward. "Humans are polluting the air that most of us
breathe. They're cutting down our
trees." "And spoiling our waters," the turtle
said. "There are fewer flowers to pollinate," the bee
said. "But how can I
help?" "We must remind them of something," the pig
said. "This is our home, the only home we
have. So we need a human
ambassador." "Oh, I get it!" The bee
nodded. "Wait, actually, I
don't." "Humans forgot how to talk to animals long ago," the magpie
said. "Now we need a very special
human." "Someone with a good heart," the turtle
added. "We believe we've found that person," the magpie
said. "She's only a child, but that's for the
best. A child is more likely to accept our gift.
And when she grows up . . ."
"She might change the world," the elephant said.
"She might convince her fellow humans to take better care of the planet we share."
"Cool!" The bee buzzed happily, and then stopped.
"But why am I here?"
"You will carry our gift to this young human," the magpie said.
"Me?" The bee covered her face with her wings.
"I can't do that!"
"Yes, you can," the elephant said.
"You are fast, small, and part of the natural habitat.
You'll use your stinger—and our magic."
She gestured toward a tide pool that glowed with magic energy.
"I have to sting someone?" the bee said.
"I don't like to do that!"
"We don't want to hurt the human child," the turtle said.
"But this is the only way to pass our magic to her."
"We're relying on you to guide her well," the magpie said.
"She could be our last chance.
It takes many years for the tide pool to build up enough magic for this."
"Do not tell her about the council!" the pig warned.
"If you do, the magic will weaken.
And please return in one week to report on our experiment."
Everyone looked at the bee.
"Will you do it?" the turtle asked.
The bumblebee was so nervous, her wings quivered.
But she knew it was an honor to be chosen. "Yes!"
She dipped her stinger into the tide pool.
The elephant waved her trunk, and then . . . Poof!
The bumblebee disappeared.
Poof! The bumblebee reappeared.
She was at the edge of a forest by a suburban backyard.
A girl named Daisy Lewis was in that backyard.
So was her best friend, Kaleem Carter, who lived next door.
They were sprawled on the grass, painting cardboard signs.
"Hand me the purple glitter paint, please," Daisy said.
"I want our names to really pop!"
The friends were making signs to advertise their pet-sitting and dog-walking business.
Daisy was only ten years old.
But everyone said she was very responsible and had a way with animals.
She couldn't have a pet of her own because of her dad's asthma.
But she loved taking care of other people's animals.
Kaleem was going to help her.
"I'll paint a fish tank on this sign." Kaleem reached for the blue paint.
He'd painted a cat and dog on some other signs.
"Thanks," Daisy said.
"Can you paint a parrot too?
I want people to know we can take care of all kinds of animals."
"Of course I can paint a parrot," Kaleem said.
"I can paint any—aah!"
Kaleem dropped his paintbrush and jumped to his feet.
He waved his arms wildly.
"What's wrong?" Daisy asked.
"There's a bee!" Kaleem looked terrified.
"I forgot to bring my EpiPen outside.
I can't get stung!"
Now Daisy understood why her friend was so upset.
Kaleem was allergic to bee stings.
And he didn't have his EpiPen–a medical device to protect him if he got stung.
"There it is!" Kaleem swatted at something in the air. "Got it!"
The bee fell to the ground.
"Don't hurt it!" Daisy rushed closer.
"There's a nicer way to shoo it away."
"Maybe for you!" Kaleem laughed nervously.
"Every animal we see loves you. But bees are pests.
And if that one stings me, I could end up in the hospital!"
"Bees aren't pests." Daisy bent down to look for the fallen insect.
"They're an important part of our ecosystem.
They help pollinate the food we eat.
Bumblebees like that one are native to the United States.
Some types are endangered!"
"Thanks for the lecture, Professor." Kaleem rolled his eyes.
"But I'll be endangered if that bee stings me!"
Daisy finally located the bee.
It was clinging to a blade of grass.
Luckily it looked okay.
Daisy gently picked it up.
"Sorry about that, little bee," Daisy said.
"Please leave my friend Kaleem alone, okay?
He's allergic to your sting."
The bee buzzed up into the air.
"I'm not here for Kaleem. I'm here for you!" she said.
But all Daisy and Kaleem heard was loud buzzing.
"The bee sounds kind of mad." Kaleem looked nervous again.
"I'd better go inside until it buzzes away."
"Get your EpiPen while you're there," Daisy said.
Kaleem ran off, and Daisy went back to painting.
Suddenly she heard the bee buzzing closer.
Then she felt it land on the back of her neck.
"Ouch!" she cried. "Hey, you stung me!"
"I'm sorry," a voice said.
"I had to do it."
"Who said that?" Daisy rubbed her neck.
Her skin felt tingly from the bee sting.
"Me." The bumblebee was hovering nearby.
"I must be hearing imaginary voices," Daisy said.
"I hope that doesn't mean I'm allergic to bee stings too!"
"Don't be silly."
The bumblebee buzzed in a circle.
"I'm not imaginary. I'm real, like you."
Daisy blinked.
She knew she shouldn't believe this was happening.
But she loved books and movies where people and animals could talk to each other.
She wanted it to be true.
"Okay, maybe this is real.
If you can understand me, fly to the garden shed and back."
The bee let out a tiny sigh.
"We don't have time for games, I have to get you to . . . Uh, I mean, okay, fine."
The bee buzzed across the yard.
She landed briefly on the garden shed and returned.
"Wow!" Daisy cried.
"So, can I understand all bees, or only you?"
"Not just me, and not just bees.
You can talk with all animals now."
"What?" Daisy gasped.
Just then a bird landed nearby.
"I'm hungry," he sang. "So hungry!"
Daisy grinned.
She understood the bird too!
"Mr. Smith has lots of bird feeders in his yard."
Daisy pointed across the street.
The bird looked at her in surprise.
"Thank you!" He flew away.
"This is amazing!" Daisy said.
"I never thought I'd thank a bee for stinging me!
I'm Daisy. What's your name?"
The bee flapped her wings uncertainly.
"Bees don't have names."
"Hmm," Daisy said. "What if I call you Beatrice?"
"Beatrice. That sounds like 'bee.'"
The bee sounded pleased. "I like it!"
"So, how did you do this, Beatrice?
Are you a magic bee?"
"Magic? Who told you there was magic?
I never said anything about magic!" Beatrice sounded flustered.
"Er, I shouldn't . . . that is . . . Excuse me, I'd better go check on my . . . colony."
"That was strange," Daisy thought as Beatrice left.
"Daisy!" Kaleem ran toward her.
"Kaleem! You'll never believe what just happened!" Daisy said.
"You can tell me later." Kaleem looked worried.
"Dumpling escaped! She must have sneaked out when I opened the door.
The last time she got out, she didn't come home for two days."
Dumpling was Kaleem's cat.
"Don't worry, we'll find her," Daisy said.
"It'll be easy, because I can talk to animals now."
"What?" Kaleem frowned.
"This is no time for weird jokes. Come on!
I saw her run toward the forest."
Daisy followed as he hurried away.
She tried to tell him about Beatrice again.
But he still thought she was kidding around.
"I'm telling the truth."
Daisy spotted a squirrel up a tree.
"Hey, squirrel, have you seen a cat out here?"
The squirrel paused.
"I smelled one. That's why I'm hiding up here."
He scampered higher.
Daisy told Kaleem what the squirrel had said.
"Stop it!" Kaleem sounded even more annoyed.
"We have to find Dumpling!"
"I know where your cat is!" a tiny voice squeaked.
Daisy bent down.
A mouse was trembling near her feet.
"Your cat ran past," he said.
"I barely had time to hide!
She climbed that maple tree just ahead."
"This mouse says Dumpling is in that tree."
Daisy pointed to the maple.
"I told you, stop joking around," Kaleem said.
"This is serious!"
Daisy squinted at the top of the maple. "Dumpling?"
"I'm here!" a voice called.
"But I'm stuck!"
Kaleem gasped.
"It's Dumpling!"
"You mean you heard her too?" Daisy asked in surprise.
Kaleem nodded. "Dumpling meows really loudly."
"She wasn't meowing," Daisy said.
"She was talking
." Kaleem ignored
Daisy. "I'm here! Come down,
Dumpling!" "I can't!" the cat
said. "I'm good at climbing
up. But I can't figure out how to climb
down." "Look at the branch next to you," Daisy
said. "Walk halfway out. Then jump down to the next
branch." "Here, kitty!" Kaleem said. "Just come to
me!" "I'd do that if I could fly like a
bird." Dumpling sounded
grumpy. "But I'm a cat,
remember?" Daisy
laughed. "Why are you laughing?" Kaleem
asked. Daisy realized he really couldn't understand Dumpling's
words. "Never
mind." Dumpling began following Daisy's
directions. Once Dumpling was on the lower branch, Daisy kept directing
her. Finally the cat was low enough to jump to the
ground. "Good kitty!" Kaleem scooped her
up. "You followed my
voice." "If you say so," Dumpling
said. "I'm just happy to be
down. I could use a snack and a
nap." Daisy told Kaleem what the cat had
said. He frowned. "Why do you keep making this joke? It's not funny."
"It's not a joke," Daisy said.
As they walked back home, she explained again.
"Everyone knows you're good with animals, Daisy.
But you're not Doctor Dolittle, the guy in that book we read in school."
The Story of Doctor Dolittle was one of Daisy's favorite books.
The main character could talk to all kinds of animals.
And now she could too!
Daisy groaned.
"How can I convince you?
Oh, here's Beatrice, the bee who stung me."
"Tell her not to sting me," Kaleem said nervously.
"She knows you're allergic," Daisy said.
"Wait—does this mean you believe me?"
Kaleem rolled his eyes. "No!"
"Beatrice, I need to convince Kaleem I can talk to animals," Daisy said.
"Would you please fly around my head?"
Beatrice sighed. "I don't know.
Is that against the rules?"
"What rules?" Daisy asked.
"Oops! Um, nothing . . . I mean, uh, okay."
Beatrice circled Daisy's head.
Kaleem shrugged. "That's not really proof.
Bees fly around all the time."
Suddenly Dumpling spoke up.
"Tell him I saw him put on dinosaur underwear this morning."
Daisy giggled.
"Dumpling says you're wearing dinosaur underwear. Is that true?"
"Whoa! How do you know that?" Kaleem looked shocked.
Then he looked amazed. "Did Dumpling really tell you that?
I should have known you would never lie to me, Daisy.
You can talk to animals!"
"That's what I've been trying to tell you!" Daisy grinned.
"I guess now you can call me Daisy Dolittle!"
"This is awesome," Kaleem said for about the twentieth time.
He and Daisy were hanging up their pet-sitting signs around the neighborhood.
"It's like something from a movie—no, from a book.
You can talk to animals just like Doctor Dolittle!"
"It's cool, right?" Daisy grinned.
"I already love animals. Now I can talk to them."
Kaleem looked excited.
"Everybody is going to freak out when you tell them."
"Tell him to calm down," Beatrice said.
"You're not supposed to tell other people."
Daisy looked at the bumblebee. "What do you mean?"
"Nothing!" Beatrice zipped back and forth.
"I'm just a bee. Sometimes I say silly things."
"Hey, that reminds me, Beatrice," Daisy said.
"You never told me how this happened.
How did your sting make me understand animals?"
Beatrice buzzed in a zigzag pattern.
"Do you smell that?
There are some flowers that need pollinating.
I, uh, better go!" She flew away at top speed.
"Where's she going?" Kaleem asked.
"To pollinate flowers, I guess," Daisy said.
"She keeps buzzing off whenever I ask about my new power."
Kaleem shrugged. "Who cares how you got it?
It's amazing! Let's go find more animals for you to talk to."
"After we finish hanging up these pet-sitting signs," Daisy said.
Kaleem's face lit up. "I just realized something!
We don't need these signs anymore.
We don't need a pet-sitting business at all.
You can use your new super power to get rich!
You could go on TV, or get your own video channel on the internet.
You could even join the circus."
"I don't want to tell everyone about this yet," Daisy said.
"I mean, it took forever to get you to believe me.
And you're my best friend. Plus, the power could wear off."
"Oh," Kaleem said. "Do you really think that might happen?"
"I don't know," Daisy said.
"I don't even know how it happened in the first place!"
As she taped a sign to a lamppost, a chickadee landed on top of it.
"What's that?" she chirped.
Daisy smiled up at the tiny bird.
"Hello, little chickadee.
We're hanging signs for our new business."
She didn't notice that a boy was walking up behind her.
"Why are you talking to birds? Are you a birdbrain?"
"Very funny, Parker," Daisy said with a frown.
"Birdbrain! Birdbrain!" Parker chanted.
"Daisy Lewis is a birdbrain!"
Parker Channing was the worst bully in their school.
He was mean to everyone.
"Go away, we're busy," Kaleem said.
"I know what would make this sign much better."
Parker dug a stubby pencil out of his pocket.
He used it to draw a big mustache on a dog Kaleem had painted.
"Hey, stop that!" Daisy cried.
"Make me!" Parker ran off, snickering loudly.
Daisy took the sign down. "He ruined it!"
"I can fix it," Kaleem said. "I'll just paint over it."
Before Daisy could answer, she heard a dog barking loudly from across the street.
"Help!" the dog barked.
"I'm alone—and scared!"
Daisy looked both ways to make sure no cars were coming.
Then she hurried across the street.
Kaleem followed. "What's wrong?"
"That dog says he's alone and scared," Daisy said.
"How can we get to him?"
The barking was coming from behind a pretty blue house with a fence.
Kaleem looked at the house next door.
"Grace Chang from our class lives there.
We went to her birthday party there last year, remember?"
"I remember," Daisy said.
"Maybe we can see the dog from her backyard."
They knocked on the door.
Grace's mother answered.
"Oh, hello. Grace is playing out back."
Grace looked surprised to see the visitors.
"Hi," she said shyly.
"Hi, Grace," Daisy and Kaleem said.
In the neighboring yard, the dog was still barking for help.
"It's okay," Daisy called, hurrying to the fence.
"I'll help you if I can."
But the dog was barking so loudly, he didn't hear her.
Grace gave Daisy an odd look.
"Are you talking to Scamp?
I don't know what's wrong.
Usually he hardly barks at all."
"So you know him?" Daisy asked.
Grace nodded. "I take care of him whenever Mrs. Ortiz goes to visit her grandkids."
Daisy wanted to tell her what Scamp was saying.
But she didn't know Grace very well.
What if Grace didn't believe her?
"Distract her for a second," she whispered to Kaleem.
Kaleem nodded.
"Hey, Grace, is that your old swing set?" he asked loudly.
"I miss swing sets! Can we play on it?"
"Um, sure." Grace looked confused.
But she led Kaleem over to the swing set.
Daisy leaned over the fence and looked around the yard.
Dog toys were scattered around, and a kiddie pool was filled with water.
But the dog wasn't paying attention to those things.
He was running back and forth near the back door.
"Help! Help!" he barked.
"Hey, Scamp!" Daisy called.
"What's wrong?"
He still didn't hear her.
The chickadee landed on the fence.
"Maybe I can help."
"Thanks," Daisy said.
The chickadee flew over and chirped at Scamp.
But he didn't pay any attention.
"Oh well, thanks for trying," Daisy said when the bird returned.
"I have another idea," the chickadee said.
"I'll be right back."
Moments later she returned with a second bird.
"Hi, I'm a catbird. Let me try."
The catbird flew over Scamp and gave his call.
It sounded like a cat meowing.
Finally Scamp looked up.
"Where's the cat?
I like playing with cats!"
"Scamp! I'm Daisy. I want to know why you're scared."
Scamp pricked up his ears and turned toward her.
"You can understand me?" He ran over to the fence.
"I love spending the morning running around the yard and playing in my pool.
I really love playing in the water!" His tail wagged briefly.
Then it drooped. "Normally my lady dries me off and brings me inside around now.
But that didn't happen today."
"Why not?" Daisy asked.
"I don't know." Scamp shot a glance at the house.
"But something is wrong—I can smell it!"
Daisy ran over to Grace.
"I think something happened to your neighbor!"
"Why do you think that?" Grace asked.
Daisy traded a look with Kaleem.
"Well, um, her dog sounds upset," Kaleem said.
"Maybe we should check on her."
"Scamp does seem anxious today," Grace said.
"He's usually really happy.
I guess it wouldn't hurt to check on Mrs. Ortiz, just in case.
She's a very nice neighbor."
They went back through Grace's house and over to Mrs. Ortiz's front door.
Daisy knocked, but nobody answered.
"Let's try again," Kaleem said. "Louder!"
Daisy knocked as hard as she could, but there was still no response.
"I guess she's not home," Grace said with a shrug.
The friendly chickadee flew over just in time to hear Grace.
"Is she talking about the old lady who lives here?" the bird asked.
"I just looked in through the window.
She's lying very still on the floor."
Daisy gasped. "Oh, no!"
Grace looked surprised. "What's wrong?"
"Which window?" Daisy asked the bird.
Now Grace looked confused.
But Daisy wasn't paying attention.
The chickadee flew over and pecked on a window nearby.
Daisy ran over and looked through it.
An older woman was lying on the floor, not moving.
"Is that Mrs. Ortiz?" Daisy cried.
Grace and Kaleem ran over.
"We shouldn't be looking through people's windows," Grace said, hanging back.
Kaleem stepped to the window.
"Oh, no!" he cried.
"Maybe she fainted or fell or something."
Grace finally looked in too.
"Mrs. Ortiz! Let's tell my parents to call for help."
They ran back to Grace's house.
Her parents were in the living room.
A huge tropical fish tank took up most of one wall.
Daisy took a deep breath.
"Mrs. Ortiz's dog was barking a lot, so we went to check on her."
"Yeah," Kaleem said.
"We thought he, um, might be trying to tell us something."
Grace's mom chuckled.
"I'm sure Scamp is just barking because he's happy.
He loves playing in the pool Mrs. Ortiz got for him."
"But we saw her," Grace said.
"Through the window. She's lying on the floor and not moving."
"You peeked in her window?" Grace's dad sounded disapproving.
But Grace's mom looked alarmed. "Which window?"
The two adults rushed out.
Daisy, Kaleem, and Grace followed.
Scamp was still barking.
"What's happening? Is my lady all right?"
"It's okay, Scamp," Daisy called back.
"We're checking on her."
Grace gave Daisy another odd look.
But she didn't say anything.
Meanwhile Grace's dad was knocking on the door.
"Mrs. Ortiz?" he called. "Are you all right?"
Grace's mom peered in through the window.
"Oh, no! We need to call for an ambulance!"
While the adults made the call, Daisy hurried to tell Scamp what was happening.
"Thank you," Scamp barked.
A moment later his ears pricked up. "I hear a siren."
Daisy couldn't hear anything.
But she knew that dogs' hearing was much better than humans' hearing.
"Phew!" she said. "Help is on the way!"
Soon paramedics were moving Mrs. Ortiz to an ambulance.
She struggled to sit up as she passed the kids.
"Grace, honey," she said weakly.
"Will you take care of Scamp while I'm in the hospital?"
"Of course," Grace said.
"I hope it won't be too much trouble," Mrs. Ortiz said.
"I know your big, beautiful fish tank takes up a lot of your time."
"Kaleem and I can help."
Daisy held up one of the signs she'd dropped outside Grace's house.
"We're pet sitters."
Mrs. Ortiz smiled.
"Wonderful. I'm sure you kids will take good care of my good boy."
Soon the ambulance drove away.
Grace's mom and dad went inside.
"Let's go tell Scamp what . . . ," Daisy began.
"Uh, I mean, let's go check on Scamp."
"Yikes!" Daisy thought.
"I almost gave away my secret!"
Kaleem looked worried, but luckily Grace didn't react to Daisy's words.
"Let's get Scamp's spare leash from my house," Grace said.
"We can take him for a walk."
In the living room, Grace's mother looked up.
"Where are you going, Grace?
You said you'd clean the fish tank this afternoon, remember?"
"Can't I do it after we take Scamp for a walk?" Grace asked.
"Your friends can do that," her father said.
"The fish are your responsibility."
Daisy stepped closer to see the fish.
One swam slowly toward her.
"Oh, look, someone new is admiring our beauty," the fish said, sounding bored.
A second fish drifted closer. "It's about time."
He blew a lazy stream of bubbles.
"Nobody pays nearly enough attention to how lovely we are."
"Well, I think you're gorgeous!" Daisy whispered.
The first fish stared at her. "That's nice.
The other girl hardly looks at us."
"I'm sorry," Daisy said.
"We don't really care." A third fish bubbled.
"We know we're stunning, and that's what's important."
"Well, that and getting fed," the first fish said.
"And having our tank cleaned."
Grace came over, looking sad.
"I have to take care of my fish now.
Can you still take Scamp for a walk?
I promise I'll feed him later."
"Sure," Daisy said. "Come on, Kaleem."
Soon they were walking Scamp through the neighborhood.
Daisy told the dog about Mrs. Ortiz going to the hospital.
"When will she come home?" Scamp asked, sounding worried.
"I don't know," Daisy said. "But we'll—"
"Squirrel!" Scamp barked suddenly.
"Squirrel, squirrel!"
"Go away, you dumb canine!" A squirrel chattered from a tree.
Daisy laughed.
"What's so funny?" Kaleem asked.
Before she could answer, Beatrice buzzed toward them.
"There you are, Beatrice! I wondered where you went," Daisy said.
"You missed something big.
I used my new power to help an animal.
I ended up helping a person too."
Beatrice landed on Daisy's hand. "Great! It's working already!"
"Huh? What's working?" Daisy asked.
"Oh, um, nothing!" Beatrice buzzed. "I have to go!"
As Beatrice sped away, Daisy sighed.
"Again? Talking to a bee can be so confusing."
She bent down to pat Scamp.
"But luckily, Scamp, I understood you perfectly!"
On Sunday morning Daisy's dad made pancakes for breakfast.
"I made yours in animal shapes, Daisy," he said. "Like always!"
"Thanks, Dad."
Daisy wondered if she should tell her parents she could talk to animals.
She normally told them everything.
But she wasn't sure they would believe her this time.
Her mom's phone rang.
"Oh, hello, Troy. Yes, she's right here."
She handed Daisy the phone. "It's for you, Daisy."
Daisy didn't have her own phone yet.
She'd put her mom's number on the pet-sitting signs.
The caller was named Troy.
He was a student at the college where Daisy's mom worked.
"Hi, Daisy. I broke my leg playing rugby," he said.
"My dog has too much energy to stay in the yard. Can you walk him for me?"
"Of course!" Daisy said. "Kaleem and I will be right over."
After she finished eating, she ran over to Kaleem's house.
"I still don't understand why we're pet sitting," Kaleem said.
"You could make tons of money talking to animals."
Dumpling was listening.
"Kaleem thinks he should be able to understand us too," she said to Daisy.
"He kept trying to talk to me last night."
Daisy giggled. Kaleem didn't ask why she was laughing.
He was looking nervously past her.
"Here comes that bee," he said.
"Make sure she knows not to sting me."
"Tell him I already know that!"
Beatrice landed on the headband Daisy was wearing.
"She looks like a pin my mom used to wear," Kaleem said.
"It was shaped like a beetle. That's almost like a bee."
"Is he kidding?" Beatrice sounded insulted.
"Bumblebees help flowers and other plants grow.
Beetles just like to eat them!"
When they reached Troy's house, he was sitting on the stoop.
His leg was in a cast.
A cute, mixed-breed dog was beside him, chewing on a stick.
"Thanks for coming," Troy said.
"Finn is used to a long walk every day.
He loves chewing on sticks and playing ball in the park."
"I also love smelling everything at the park," Finn barked.
"There are tons of interesting smells there."
After Troy went inside, Daisy smiled at Finn.
"Hi, I'm Daisy. Don't worry, I'll let you smell as many things as you want."
Finn pranced all around.
"You understood what I said? Wow, wow, wow!
A human who can talk with animals! That's great!"
Daisy laughed. Finn was very energetic!
She and Kaleem took Finn to the park.
They tossed a ball for him.
Finn also sniffed everything he saw.
He told Daisy all about what he was smelling.
"This was fun," Daisy said at last.
"But we should get you home now."
"Do we have to go home?" Finn dropped his head.
"My favorite chew toy disappeared last night.
Without it, I'm afraid I'll start chewing on the patio furniture.
Troy gets upset when I do that."
"Hmm, your chew toy disappeared?" Daisy said.
"Maybe we can help you find it."
"Maybe," Finn said.
"But I think Hazel—the dog next door—stole it!"
Kaleem clipped on Finn's leash, and they headed back to Troy's house.
Daisy told Kaleem about Finn's problem.
"Finn, are you sure Hazel stole your chew toy?" Daisy asked.
"Yes! Hazel's owner doesn't let her leave toys in the yard.
That's why I think she took mine."
"We'll go ask her after we drop you off," Daisy said.
"What does your missing toy look like?"
"It's shaped like a doughnut," Finn said.
"It squeaks when I bite it."
Troy was waiting for them.
He patted Finn and handed Daisy some money.
"Thanks," he said.
"Can you walk Finn again tomorrow?"
"I'll come right after school. He's a great dog."
Daisy gave Finn a hug.
While she did, she whispered in his ear.
"We'll come back sooner if we find your chew toy."
Finn wagged his tail. "I'll try not to chew anything until you find it.
But I can't make any promises."
Daisy just nodded and winked at him.
She didn't want Troy to guess her secret.
After Troy and Finn went inside, Daisy and Kaleem went next door.
An old poodle was lying on the porch.
